title: How ants find the shortest way
interaction: Ants wander out of a nest at random; one that finds the sugar walks home laying a scent, and the others follow scent rather than chance, so a trail forms and thickens. Drag the sugar farther away or drop a pebble on the trail and watch the colony reroute. Then offer a long bridge and a short one to the same food and count the ants on each: the short one wins because its scent is refreshed more often, and with the scent's fading switched off the colony stays stuck on whichever bridge it found first.
takeaway: A colony finds the shortest path with no map and no ant that knows it: a scent that fades rewards the route that gets walked most often.
pitfall: No ant knows where the food is or compares the routes, and the queen gives no orders; real ants also use sight and memory, which the page leaves out and says so.
why: The NetLogo Ants model, a standard classroom agent model of pheromone trails (Deneubourg's double-bridge experiment): https://ccl.northwestern.edu/netlogo/models/Ants
overlapWith: graph-search: an algorithm explores a map systematically to find the shortest route; this page finds one with many simple agents and a fading scent, with no map at all.
needsSource: none

title: Why a cut apple goes brown
interaction: A cut apple face, drawn as a sheet of cells. Scrub the minutes and brown spreads in from wherever air touches the cut, because an enzyme freed by the cut meets the air, while a brownness meter climbs. One control at a time: paint a region with lemon juice (the enzyme stops in acid), press cling film over a region (no air), move the apple into the fridge (slower), or dip a slice in boiling water (the enzyme is destroyed). Each region browns at its own pace side by side.
takeaway: An apple browns because a cut lets one of its own enzymes meet the air, so keeping air off, chilling it, or lemon juice each slow the browning, and heat stops it for good.
needsSource: none; a cut-surface grid with air diffusing in and an enzyme rate that depends on acidity and temperature (constants from the polyphenol-oxidase references)
pitfall: Browning is not rotting and not the apple going bad: a brown apple slice is safe. And lemon juice does not 'seal' the surface; it stops the enzyme.
why: Science Buddies 'Enzymatic Browning' activity (apple and banana, lemon juice): https://www.sciencebuddies.org/stem-activities/enzymatic-browning
overlapWith: the-cell: this page's cells are only the containers a cut breaks open, and the-cell never shows an enzyme at work; its browning is also unrelated to the dry-heat browning of toast.

title: A bean in a jar
interaction: A bean seed pressed against the glass of a jar with a wet paper towel. One control at a time: water or none, warm or cold, light or a dark cupboard. Scrub the days and the seed swells, splits, sends a root down and a shoot up while a growth ruler follows. No water and nothing happens; cold and it takes weeks; in the dark it sprouts just as well but the seedling grows pale and leggy, then stops once its stored food is used up, while the one in the light turns green and keeps going. Turn the jar on its side and the root bends down again.
takeaway: A seed needs water and warmth, not light, to sprout, because it lives on food stored inside it, and only once that runs out does the seedling need light to make its own.
needsSource: none; a germination and growth rate against temperature and water with a stored-food budget, constants from published bean germination studies
pitfall: Seeds do not need light or soil to germinate, and a seedling in the dark grows taller, not shorter, at first; that is not healthy growth but stored food running out.
why: England KS2 Year 3 'Plants' (requirements for life and growth) and NGSS 3-LS1-1 (life cycles): https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study (curriculum page; not fetched this session, search budget exhausted)
overlapWith: photosynthesis: that page runs the chloroplast with light and CO2 at level 1; here light matters only after the seed's stored food is gone, and the controls are water, warmth and a dark cupboard.

title: Bread and yeast
interaction: A ball of dough in a bowl, with a window into it: yeast cells drawn as dots eat sugar particles and give off gas particles that collect in bubbles, so the dough swells and a ruler follows it. One control: the temperature of the room. Cold and the yeast barely move; warm and the dough doubles in an hour; too hot and the yeast die and the rise stops for good. A second run bakes the dough: the oven swells the bubbles once more and then sets the crumb, and the baked slice shows its holes.
takeaway: Dough rises because living yeast eat sugar and breathe out gas that gets trapped in the dough, fastest when it is warm but not hot, and the holes in bread are those bubbles.
needs: Rate of gas production by baker's yeast against temperature, from a published fermentation study (a cardinal-temperature curve with a few fitted constants); no dataset.
needsSource: A few fitted constants from a published yeast fermentation-rate study; facts, no dataset
pitfall: Yeast is alive and does not simply 'activate': too much heat kills it, and the holes in bread are not air mixed in by kneading.
why: Demand: 'why does yeast make bread rise' (BBC Science Focus): https://www.sciencefocus.com/nature/why-does-yeast-make-bread-rise/; England KS2 Year 6 'Living things' (micro-organisms) and NGSS MS-LS1-1.
overlapWith: respiration-atp: that page follows glucose through the cell at level 2; here the yeast is a dot that eats sugar and makes a bubble, and the only control is warmth.

title: Caterpillar to butterfly
interaction: Step a monarch from egg to butterfly on a day counter: the caterpillar eats and swells until its skin, which cannot stretch, splits and is shed, five times over, growing about two thousand times heavier in two weeks; then it hangs, sheds once more into a chrysalis, and a cutaway shows most of its insides dissolved and rebuilt into wings, legs and a drinking straw while the stored fat drains. Warm the days and every stage runs faster.
takeaway: A caterpillar is an eating machine that must shed its skin to grow, and inside the chrysalis it is largely taken apart and rebuilt into a flying one.
needsSource: none: growth across five instars with a moult whenever the body outgrows its skin, a mass budget in the pupa, and stage lengths versus temperature from the monarch literature (Monarch Joint Venture; Zalucki 1982), stated on the page
pitfall: The caterpillar does not turn to soup: its nervous system, some muscles and the small clusters of cells that become the wings survive and build the adult, and the butterfly is the same individual, not a new one.
why: England KS2 Year 5 statutory requirement: describe the differences in the life cycles of a mammal, an amphibian, an insect and a bird. https://www.ase.org.uk/sites/default/files/PLAN%20Examples%20of%20Work%20Y5%20Living%20things%20and%20their%20habitats%20Melissa.pdf
overlapWith: the-cell: that page shows what a cell contains; this one follows one animal's body being rebuilt, as masses and moults, with no cell biology.

title: Fireflies that flash together
interaction: A meadow of fireflies, each with its own inner clock that flashes when it strikes twelve and starts again. One control: how much a neighbour's flash nudges a firefly's clock forward. At zero the meadow twinkles at random; turn it up and patches start flashing together, then waves, then the whole field as one; drag a finger through the swarm to scramble it and watch it fall back into step.
takeaway: Thousands of fireflies flash together with no conductor, because each one nudges its own clock a little toward every flash it sees.
pitfall: There is no lead firefly and no outside signal; synchrony appears only from each insect reacting to its neighbours. Only some firefly species do this.
why: Nicky Case's 'Fireflies' explorable (public domain), the interactive credited in Veritasium's synchronization video: https://ncase.me/fireflies/
overlapWith: oscillations-resonance: one oscillator pushed at a frequency; this page is many self-timed flashers nudging each other into step, which is not resonance. kuramoto-synchronization (this batch, level 3) is the grown-up phase-coupled model.
needsSource: none

title: Flocks without a leader
interaction: A hundred birds fly across the stage following three rules, each drawn as a short arrow on one highlighted bird: keep a little distance from your neighbours, fly the way they fly, drift toward the middle of them. Switch one rule off at a time: without the first the birds pile into clumps, without the second the flock never agrees on a direction, without the third it scatters. Add a hawk and watch the flock split around it and close again with no bird in charge.
takeaway: A flock keeps its shape because every bird follows the same three simple rules about its nearest neighbours, not because any bird leads.
pitfall: No bird leads or sees the whole flock; each reacts only to its few nearest neighbours, and the shapes of a murmuration are planned by nobody.
why: NGSS 3-LS2-1 (some animals form groups that help members survive); Reynolds's boids is the classic classroom model of it (MIT StarLogo activity): https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/3-ls2-1-ecosystems-interactions-energy-and-dynamics
overlapWith: ecosystems: populations tied together by birth and predation rates; this page is the movement of one group where each animal follows a rule about its neighbours, with no population counts at all.
needsSource: none

title: Flowers and bees
interaction: Watch bees work a meadow of flowers: each visit leaves pollen from the last flower and picks up new, and a flower only sets seed once pollen from another of its kind has arrived; count the seed heads at the end of the day. Take the bees away, paint the flowers dull, or thin the meadow, and count again.
takeaway: A flower cannot move, so it pays bees in sugar to carry its pollen, and without the bees most of the seeds never form.
needsSource: none: an agent simulation of bees drawn to colour and scent, carrying pollen that is deposited and diluted at each visit, with seed set requiring pollen of the right kind and nectar that refills over time
pitfall: Bees are not helping on purpose and flowers are not for people: each is feeding, and the pollen hitches a ride. Not every flower needs a bee: grasses and many trees use the wind.
why: England KS2 Year 3 statutory requirement: explore the part that flowers play in the life cycle of flowering plants, including pollination, seed formation and seed dispersal. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: ecosystems: that page couples a predator and its prey; this one couples two species that trade, counted in seeds, with no population cycles.

title: Who eats whom
interaction: Drag plants and animals from a shelf into a chain, grass to grasshopper to frog to hawk, and the arrows point the way the food goes; then feed it: a thousand plants feed about a hundred grasshoppers, ten frogs and one hawk, and the pyramid of counts builds itself. Cross two chains into a web, remove the grass or add a second hawk, and watch how many of each the field can feed.
takeaway: Each step up a food chain feeds about ten times fewer animals, which is why a field holds a thousand grass plants, a hundred grasshoppers, ten frogs and one hawk.
needsSource: none: an energy-budget pyramid with a transfer fraction of about one tenth per link (Lindeman 1942, a rule of thumb stated as such) and example daily intakes from textbook ecology
pitfall: Arrows point from the food to the eater, the direction the energy goes, not from the eater to the eaten. And the one-tenth is a rule of thumb, not a law: the page says about.
why: NGSS 5-LS2-1: develop a model to describe the movement of matter among plants, animals, decomposers and the environment; also England KS2 Year 4 food chains. https://keslerscience.com/ngss-5-ls2-1-cycling-of-matter
overlapWith: ecosystems: that page runs predator and prey through time and removes species from a web; this one has no time at all, only arrows and counts, the door to that page.

title: How a fridge keeps food fresh
interaction: A plate of food with a count of germs on it, starting at a handful. One control: where the plate sits (a warm kitchen, a cool room, the fridge, the freezer), set by dragging the plate. Scrub the hours and days: on the counter the count doubles every half hour or so and passes the 'unsafe' line in hours; in the fridge each doubling takes many hours and the line is reached in days; in the freezer the count stands still. Move a plate from the freezer back to the counter and the doubling resumes from where it stopped.
takeaway: Cold does not kill the germs on food; it slows how often they double, so the same food lasts hours on the counter, days in the fridge, and months in the freezer.
needs: Bacterial growth rate against temperature for a common spoilage bacterium (the Ratkowsky square-root model and its fitted constants; Ratkowsky et al., J. Bacteriol. 1982 and 1983, free to read on PMC), plus the USDA FSIS 'danger zone' limits (public domain).
needsSource: Fitted constants from Ratkowsky et al. 1982/1983 (free on PMC; a few numbers, not a dataset) and USDA FSIS limits (public domain)
pitfall: Freezing does not kill bacteria and the fridge does not 'clean' food: thawed food carries every germ it froze with, and cooking is what kills them.
why: USDA FSIS 'Danger Zone' guidance (bacteria double in as little as 20 minutes between 40 and 140 °F): https://www.fsis.usda.gov/news-events/news-press-releases/usda-urges-consumers-keep-clear-danger-zone-summer
overlapWith: epidemics: that page spreads infection between people at level 1; here germs multiply on one plate and the only control is its temperature, with nothing spreading between people.

title: How fish breathe
interaction: Push water over a gill with a slider while blood runs through it the other way, and count the oxygen dots that cross from water to blood; flip a switch to make the blood run the same way as the water and the dots that cross fall to about half. Lift the fish out of the water and the feathery gill folds collapse onto each other and dry, and the dots stop crossing.
takeaway: A fish gets oxygen by running its blood against the water flow, so the blood always meets water fresher than itself.
needsSource: none: a one-dimensional counter-current exchanger with diffusion between two flows; water holds about thirty times less oxygen per litre than air, from textbook physiology
pitfall: Fish out of water are not short of oxygen (air has more): the gill folds stick together and dry out so nothing can cross. And gills are not lungs that happen to be outside: the water flows through, it is never held.
why: NGSS 4-LS1-1: internal structures that support survival, with gills among the standard classroom examples. https://www2.cde.ca.gov/cacs/id/web/29023
overlapWith: heart-circulation: that page has one loop for the lungs; this is the gill itself as an exchanger you can run backwards, with no heart.

title: How plants drink
interaction: Stand a stick of celery or a white flower in coloured water and watch the dye climb; set the day to sunny, windy, humid or dark and the climb speeds up or stalls, because the pull comes from water leaving the leaves. Zoom to the leaf's pores opening and closing, then scale up to a tree on a hot day and count the buckets it lifts.
takeaway: A plant has no pump: the leaves let water escape into the air, and that pulls a chain of water up from the roots.
needsSource: none: cohesion-tension with a simple evaporative-demand term (light, wind, humidity, pore opening) sets the flow, and the dye front follows it; a tree's daily water use quoted from textbook plant physiology
pitfall: Roots do not push water up a tree (root pressure is tiny), and plants do not eat soil: the soil supplies water and a little mineral salt, and the plant's bulk comes from the air.
why: NGSS 5-LS1-1: plants acquire their material for growth chiefly from air and water. https://www2.cde.ca.gov/cacs/id/web/29040
overlapWith: photosynthesis: that page opens the stomata for carbon dioxide; this one follows the water those same pores let out, and nothing is made.

title: Inside an egg
interaction: Scrub the 21 days of a hen's egg in a warm incubator: candle it to watch the embryo grow, the yolk shrink and the air pocket at the blunt end widen as water seeps out through the shell's tiny holes. Turn the incubator's humidity up or down and the pocket grows too slowly or too fast; at day 21 the chick breaks into that pocket for its first breath and then through the shell.
takeaway: An egg is a packed lunch with a breathing shell: the chick eats the yolk, breathes through thousands of tiny holes, and the air pocket it needs at the end is made by the water those holes let out.
needs: A published day-by-day table of chick embryo mass (e.g. Romanoff 1960, The Avian Embryo) transcribed with citation, not yet confirmed open; the 12 percent water-loss target by day 18 comes from hatchery guides (Pas Reform, Cobb) that are published but not openly licensed; candling views drawn in-house.
needsSource: weak until a source is confirmed: the daily embryo mass curve needs a citable table (Romanoff 1960 or a poultry-science paper); water-loss targets from hatchery guides, published but not openly licensed
pitfall: A supermarket egg has no chick in it and never will: it is unfertilised. And the shell is not sealed: it breathes, which is why the air pocket grows and why a dirty or waxed egg can suffocate a chick.
why: Classroom hatching programmes (4-H embryology) with candling lessons, taught in primary schools across the US; the Year 5 bird life cycle in England. https://afs.ca.uky.edu/sites/afs.ca.uky.edu/files/Embryology%20-%20Lesson%206%20-%20Candling.pdf
overlapWith: the-cell: that page zooms into a finished cell; this one watches one cell's descendants become a chick, as masses and an air pocket, with no cell biology.

title: Jelly and the pineapple problem
interaction: A bowl of hot jelly at particle scale: long strands drifting free. Scrub it cooling in the fridge and the strands tangle into a net that holds the water still, so the bowl stops sloshing. One control: what fruit goes in. Tinned pineapple, strawberries or oranges change nothing; fresh pineapple (or kiwi) brings an enzyme that snips strands wherever it meets them, and the net never joins up however long it cools. Heat the fresh pineapple first and the enzyme is wrecked and the jelly sets.
takeaway: Jelly sets when long strands tangle into a net, and fresh pineapple carries an enzyme that cuts the strands faster than they can tangle, which cooking the pineapple stops.
needsSource: none; a strand-network model (percolation) with a cutting enzyme that heat destroys
pitfall: The pineapple does not 'melt' the jelly or add water; it cuts the strands. And tinned pineapple works because it was cooked, not because it was sweetened.
why: A standard home experiment: 'Fruit enzymes gelatin experiment' (which fruits stop jelly setting, and why cooked pineapple does not): https://teachbesideme.com/fruit-enzymes-gelatin-experiment/; England KS3 biology (enzymes in digestion).
overlapWith: protein-folding: that page folds a chain against an energy score at level 2; here strands only tangle or get cut, and the reader's control is the fruit.

title: Milk, vinegar and yogurt
interaction: A glass of milk at particle scale: protein balls drifting apart because they all carry the same charge. One control at a time: a spoon of vinegar, and the acid takes the charge away so the balls clump into curds that sink under clear whey; a spoonful of live yogurt into warm milk, and bacteria eat the milk sugar and make the acid themselves, so the same clumping happens over hours into one smooth set. A thermometer shows the yogurt bacteria working only when warm, and heating the milk first gives a thicker set.
takeaway: Milk is a cloud of tiny protein balls kept apart by their charge; acid, poured in or made by bacteria, lets them clump, which is curds in a minute or yogurt overnight.
needsSource: none; a charged-colloid clumping model with acid, plus a bacterial acid-production rate against temperature (a few published constants)
pitfall: Milk curdling with vinegar is not milk 'going off', and the bacteria in yogurt are not the bacteria that spoil food: the same clumping is cheese, yogurt and sour milk.
why: NGSS 5-PS1-4 names milk and vinegar as a mixing that makes a new substance: https://www.nextgenscience.org/dci-arrangement/5-ps1-matter-and-its-interactions; England KS2 Year 6 (micro-organisms, including useful ones).
overlapWith: acids-bases: that page tracks pH on a logarithmic scale through a titration; here acid is only something that lets protein balls stick, and the reader never sees a pH number.

title: Mould on bread
interaction: A loaf in a bread bin. Scrub a week: a spore lands, and a network of threads spreads through the crumb, shown in an x-ray view the reader can toggle; the fuzzy spot on the surface appears days after the threads beneath it, and by the time it shows the threads reach well beyond it. Pan to a second loaf kept in the fridge (slower) and a third left to dry (barely any). One control: how moist the bread is. Cut off the fuzzy spot and the x-ray shows what was left behind.
takeaway: The fuzzy spot is only the top of a mould whose threads have already spread far through the bread unseen, so cutting the spot off does not remove it; mould needs damp, and cold slows it.
needsSource: none; a thread-growth model on a grid with a moisture- and temperature-dependent extension rate, stated as a simplification
pitfall: Mould is not dirt on the surface, and a spot cut off does not make the rest of a soft loaf clean; hard cheese is different because the threads cannot push through it.
why: USDA FSIS 'Molds on Food: Are They Dangerous?' (why soft foods with a mould spot are discarded whole): https://www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/safe-food-handling-and-preparation/food-safety-basics/molds-food-are-they-dangerous (canonical page; not fetched this session, search budget exhausted); England KS2 Year 6 (micro-organisms).
overlapWith: the-cell: that page shows animal, plant and bacterial cells; a mould's thread network is a different kind of body, and no existing page shows a fungus or anything growing through food.

title: Why onions make you cry
interaction: An onion slice under a magnifier, its cells drawn as little boxes, each holding two ingredients kept in separate compartments. Drag a knife across: every cell the blade opens spills its two ingredients together, they react, and a puff of tear gas rises and drifts toward an eye whose tear count climbs. One control at a time: a sharper knife (fewer crushed cells), a chilled onion (less of the gas rises off a cold cut), cutting under running water (the gas dissolves), or a fan. Garlic in the same rig stings the nose and not the eyes.
takeaway: An onion makes its tear gas only when a cell is cut open and two ingredients kept apart inside it finally meet, so fewer crushed cells, cold, or water in the way mean fewer tears.
needsSource: none; a cell-grid model with a temperature-dependent reaction and a drifting gas, the chemistry named only in the text
pitfall: The gas is not stored in the onion waiting to escape; it is made at the moment of cutting. Chilling helps a little, and whether it slows the reaction itself is disputed, so the page must not claim it does.
why: Demand: 'why do onions make you cry' (Discover): https://www.discovermagazine.com/health/why-do-onions-make-us-cry; England KS2 Year 6 / NGSS MS-LS1-2 (cells and their parts).
overlapWith: the-cell: that page zooms through a cell's organelles; here cells are boxes that matter only because cutting them mixes what they keep apart.

title: Ripening in a paper bag
interaction: A bowl of hard green bananas and avocados. One control at a time: put them in a paper bag, add a ripe apple, or put them in the fridge. Each fruit gives off a ripening gas drawn as particles, more as it ripens, so a closed bag fills with gas and every fruit inside ripens faster, a ripe apple adds a burst, and the open bowl lets the gas drift away; cold slows everything. Scrub the days and watch the colours turn and a firmness meter fall, then overshoot into brown if left too long.
takeaway: Ripening fruit gives off a gas that tells fruit nearby to ripen too, so a bag traps it and speeds things up, an open bowl lets it escape, and cold slows it all down.
needsSource: none; a self-reinforcing ethylene production rate against ripeness and temperature, with constants from postharvest references, stated as a simplification
pitfall: The bag does not work by keeping light out or keeping the fruit warm; it keeps the fruit's own gas in. And a ripe fruit ripens its neighbours, which is why one bad apple spoils the barrel.
why: Demand: 'how to ripen avocados faster' is a top kitchen search; classroom version at education.com: https://www.education.com/activity/article/ripening-avocados
overlapWith: homeostasis: that page's feedback loop is a person's blood sugar at level 1; here a fruit's gas feeds back on its own ripening and its neighbours', and no existing page touches fruit or ethylene.

title: How a seed wakes up
interaction: Plant a bean on wet paper and set one thing at a time, water, warmth or light: the seed swells, the root pokes out and turns down, the shoot turns up, on a day counter that runs faster when it is warm and wet. Keep it in the dark and it still sprouts, pale and tall, while the food packed inside it shrinks; its weight falls until the leaves open and only then starts to climb.
takeaway: A seed needs water and warmth to wake up, not light or soil: it lives off the food packed inside it until its own leaves open.
needsSource: none: the hydrothermal-time germination model (Gummerson 1986; Bradford 2002) has no light term; the seedling's mass falls on its reserves and rises once leaves open; bean parameters stated on the page
pitfall: Seeds are not dead and do not need soil; and the seedling gets lighter, not heavier, until it can make its own food. Light matters for growing, not for sprouting.
why: NGSS 5-LS1-1, taught with bean seeds sprouting on a wet paper towel in a bag with no soil. https://thewonderofscience.com/5ls11
overlapWith: photosynthesis: that page starts once there is a leaf in the light; this one is everything before the first leaf opens.

title: Tree rings
interaction: Scrub the years of a real tree's life and watch it lay down one ring a year, wide in a good year and narrow in a dry one, drawn to the measured widths from a public archive; hover a ring for its year and its measured width, and the narrow ones are the hard years. Then try the detectives' trick: slide the ring pattern of an old beam along a living tree's record until the narrow years line up, and read off when the beam was cut.
takeaway: A tree writes one ring a year, wide in good years and narrow in bad ones, so its rings are both a calendar and a weather diary that can be matched between trees.
needs: Raw ring-width series (.rwl) from the International Tree-Ring Data Bank, NOAA NCEI World Data Service for Paleoclimatology: a US government archive, catalogued as CC0 by the Open Data Institute; each contributed series cites its authors.
needsSource: ITRDB ring-width series, NOAA NCEI (US government archive, CC0 per the ODI certificate; data.gov lists no licence, so confirm on the study page)
pitfall: Not every ring is a year everywhere: in a bad year a tree can skip a ring or add a false one, which is why the match uses a whole pattern of narrow years, never a single count.
why: Demand and data: the ITRDB is the world's largest public archive of tree-ring measurements, catalogued on data.gov. https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/noaa-wds-paleoclimatology-the-international-tree-ring-data-bank-itrdb-revisited
overlapWith: deep-time: that page scrubs Earth's whole record; this one scrubs one tree's rings, one per year, and teaches the matching trick that dates old wood.

title: Why big birds flap slowly
interaction: Pick a real bird, from a hummingbird to a swan, and see it flap at its own rate and fly at the speed it needs to stay up; drag the size slider to blow a sparrow up to goose size and watch the flap rate fall and the needed speed climb. Past a certain size the sums no longer work for flapping, and the biggest flyers are shown soaring instead.
takeaway: Bigger birds must fly faster and flap slower, and past a certain size flapping cannot keep them up, which is why the biggest flyers soar.
needs: AVONET (Tobias et al. 2022, Ecology Letters, paper CC BY 4.0; the data files on Figshare, licence to confirm) for species mass, wing length and wing area; Pennycuick's wingbeat-frequency formula (J. Exp. Biol. 1990, revised 1996) and minimum flight speed from wing loading.
needsSource: AVONET species measurements (paper CC BY 4.0, dataset licence to confirm on the repository); Pennycuick 1990/1996 published formulas
pitfall: Do not explain lift here: flight owns it, and never with equal transit time. A bird's size does not scale evenly: weight grows faster than wing area, which is the whole point.
why: Demand: the universal flapping-frequency equation made popular-science news in 2024. https://physicsworld.com/a/simple-equation-predicts-how-quickly-animals-flap-their-wings/
overlapWith: flight: that page is lift and stall on a wing section at level 2; this one never looks at the wing's shape, only at how flap rate and speed change with a bird's size across real species.

title: Why leaves change colour
interaction: Watch one maple leaf from late summer into autumn on a calendar scrub: as the days shorten and the nights cool, the green pigment is broken down and pulled back into the tree, and the yellow and orange that were underneath all along show through; sunny days with cold nights brew red on top. Then force the weather: a warm, dull autumn gives yellow without red, and an early frost cuts the show short.
takeaway: The yellow was in the leaf all summer, hidden under the green; the tree takes the green back before letting the leaf go.
needsSource: none for the model (green pigment broken down as days shorten and cool, yellow pigments constant, red made on bright cool days, leaf colour mixed from the pigments); if the colour is mixed from measured pigment spectra, PhotochemCAD's spectra are freely downloadable but their licence must be checked
pitfall: Leaves do not make yellow in autumn: the yellow was already there, and only the red is made fresh. Cold does not cause the change by itself: the shortening days are the main trigger.
why: England KS1 statutory requirement, Seasonal changes: observe changes across the four seasons; and the most-asked autumn question. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: photosynthesis: that page is the green pigment at work; this one is the green being dismantled and what it leaves behind.

title: Diffusion, osmosis & active transport
interaction: Drop dye into one corner of a box of jiggling particles and watch it spread, faster when warmer, while a concentration graph flattens. Put a membrane down the middle with pores that pass water but not sugar, set the sugar concentration on each side and watch the water level rise on the sugary side; then make the box a cell, place it in pure water, salt water and something in between, and see it swell, shrink or hold, as a potato slice does in the classroom experiment. Finally switch on a pump that carries particles against the gradient and watch its ATP meter drain.
takeaway: Particles spread from where they are crowded to where they are not by random motion alone, water does the same across a membrane that holds the dissolved particles back, and moving anything the other way costs energy.
needsSource: none
pitfall: Osmosis is water moving toward the higher solute concentration, not toward 'more water'. Diffusion needs no force or pump: particles have no direction of their own, and the net flow is a counting effect. A plant cell in pure water becomes firm rather than bursting, because of its wall.
why: AQA GCSE Biology 8461 topic 4.1.3 'Transport in cells' (diffusion, osmosis, active transport) with Required practical 3, osmosis in plant tissue https://www.edplace.com/gcse-revision/biology/aqa
overlapWith: entropy (level 2) shows two gases mixing as a count of microstates and the-cell shows the membrane as a structure; neither has a membrane that passes water and holds solute, a cell that swells or shrinks, or a pump that spends ATP. The pool's smells-and-diffusion (level 0) spreads a smell without the membrane.

title: DNA fingerprinting: matching a profile
interaction: DNA from a scene and from three suspects; at each of a dozen marker sites the DNA repeats a short word a number of times that differs between people. Step through: copy each site, sort the copies by length into peaks, and read off the repeat counts as a profile; compare profiles site by site, where one mismatch excludes a suspect and a full match is weighed by how common each count is in real population tables, the page multiplying the shares as sites are added, from one in ten with one marker to one in a billion with twelve. Mix two people's DNA and see the peaks overlap.
takeaway: A DNA profile is a list of repeat counts at a dozen or so places: most people share any one count, almost nobody shares all of them, and the odds of a chance match come from how common each count is.
needs: STR allele frequencies for a US population sample from NIST (Hill et al. 2013, 1,036 individuals, 29 loci).
pitfall: A match is a probability from population tables, not certainty, and one in a billion is the chance of a random match, not the chance the suspect is innocent. Relatives share more counts than strangers. The suspects' profiles are synthetic and labelled so; only the frequencies are real.
why: Genetic fingerprinting is in the AQA A-level Biology specification (7402, section 3.8.4.3: VNTRs, PCR, electrophoresis, forensic use), and NIST's STRBase is the reference for the method's population data: https://www.aqa.org.uk/subjects/biology/a-level/biology-7402/specification/subject-content
overlapWith: meiosis-inheritance: how variants are shuffled between generations; this page uses that variation as an identifier. gwas-polygenic-risk (pool) links variants to disease; this page only matches repeat counts between samples.
needsSource: NIST's own US population STR dataset (Hill et al. 2013): US government work, public domain. Not STRBase's compilation of published studies, whose rights vary.

title: Enzymes & digestion
interaction: Follow a meal through the mouth, stomach and small intestine while amylase, protease and lipase, drawn as lock-and-key shapes, cut starch, protein and fat into pieces small enough to cross the gut wall, with a counter of molecules absorbed. Change the temperature and the pH of each stage and watch the rate rise, peak and collapse as the enzyme's shape distorts; add bile to break fat into droplets and see the lipase rate jump with the surface area.
takeaway: Digestion is enzymes cutting big molecules into small ones, and each enzyme works fastest at one temperature and one pH and stops working when its shape is changed.
needs: Rate-against-temperature and rate-against-pH behaviour for amylase, pepsin and lipase (optimum pH near 7, 2 and 8).
needsSource: a documented Michaelis-Menten model with stated optima needs no dataset; measured constants, if wanted, from the BRENDA enzyme database (its licence was not confirmed in this research; say so before relying on it)
pitfall: Heat does not kill an enzyme, it denatures it: the protein unfolds and the active site no longer fits. Cold slows an enzyme but does not denature it. Enzymes are not used up by the reaction they speed.
why: AQA GCSE Biology 8461 topic 4.2.2.1 'The human digestive system' with Required practical 5, the effect of pH on the rate of reaction of amylase https://cognito.org/blog/gcse-aqa-biology
overlapWith: respiration-atp (level 2) follows one glucose molecule after it has been absorbed and the-cell zooms through a cell; digestion, and the enzyme as a shape that works in a narrow range of temperature and pH, is on no page. The pool's digestion-journey (level 0) is the route without the enzyme model, and its enzyme-kinetics (level 3) is the Michaelis-Menten mathematics; this page shows the behaviour between them.

title: PCR: copying DNA until there is enough to see
interaction: A tube with a few strands of DNA and a thermometer: step through one cycle (heat to split the strands, cool so short primers stick at the ends of the target, warm for the enzyme to extend them) and two strands become four; press play and the count doubles every cycle while the plot shoots up and the primers and building blocks run down. Set the starting number of copies and see when the glowing signal crosses the detection line: one copy takes about ten cycles longer than a thousand, which is how a PCR test reads how much virus was in the swab. Change the primers and a non-matching DNA stays uncopied.
takeaway: PCR copies a chosen stretch of DNA by doubling it every heating-and-cooling cycle, so thirty cycles turn a few molecules into a billion, and the cycle at which the signal appears says how many there were to start with.
pitfall: Doubling is not forever: primers and nucleotides run out and the curve flattens, so the plateau says nothing about the starting amount; only the threshold cycle does. A Ct value is not a measure of how ill someone is.
why: 'How does a PCR test work' became a mass question in 2020; public-health explainer of cycles and Ct values: https://www.publichealthontario.ca/en/About/News/2021/Explained-COVID19-PCR-Testing-and-Cycle-Thresholds
overlapWith: dna-to-protein: how DNA is read into protein; this page is how a chosen piece of DNA is copied in a tube and counted. dna-sequencing (pool, level 3) reads the letters; PCR only multiplies a chosen piece.
needsSource: none

title: Plant transport & transpiration
interaction: Set the light, temperature, humidity and wind around a potted plant and watch water drawn up its xylem from root to leaf as it evaporates from the open stomata, with a potometer bubble marking the rate; close the stomata and the flow stops. Pull a thread of water up a thin tube to see how evaporation at the top can lift a column that is never pushed, then switch to the phloem and watch sugar made in the leaf loaded in, drawing water after it, and flowing down to the roots and fruit.
takeaway: A plant has no pump: water is pulled up by evaporation from its leaves through tubes it cannot break, and sugar is pushed from leaf to root by the water it attracts.
needsSource: none; the transpiration rate is modelled from the vapour-pressure deficit and stomatal opening, documented as a simplification
pitfall: Transpiration is not a waste: it is what moves water and minerals up the plant. Roots do not push water to the top of a tree; root pressure is small and the pull from the leaves does the work.
why: AQA GCSE Biology 8461 topic 4.2.3.2 'Plant organ system' (transpiration and translocation, factors affecting the rate of transpiration) https://cognito.org/blog/gcse-aqa-biology
overlapWith: photosynthesis makes sugar in the leaf and sets light and CO2; the pool's how-plants-drink (level 0) shows water rising without the rates. This page is the plumbing: the pull of transpiration, the four factors that set its rate, and the phloem.

title: Bacterial chemotaxis
interaction: Release a few hundred E. coli into a dish with a drop of attractant and watch each one run straight, tumble, and run again; inside each cell a Barkai-Leibler receptor model sets the tumble rate, and the swarm drifts up the gradient. Move the drop, flood the dish with a uniform dose and watch the tumble rate dip then recover exactly (perfect adaptation), and change the adaptation time or the swim speed to see the biased random walk fail.
takeaway: A bacterium is too small to sense a gradient across its body, so it compares now with a moment ago and tumbles less when things are getting better; that biased random walk is enough to climb a gradient.
pitfall: The cell does not steer toward the attractant: it cannot tell direction, it only changes how often it tumbles, and the page must not draw it turning toward the source.
why: CourseSource lesson on building and simulating a chemotaxis model in Cell Collective (QUBES): https://qubeshub.org/publications/5179/
overlapWith: ecosystems: that page moves animals on a field by population rates; here each cell's movement follows an internal signalling model and the collective drift emerges from it.
needsSource: none

title: Cell cycle control
interaction: Run the Novak-Tyson model of the cyclin-Cdk switch: cyclin accumulates, Cdk activity stays low until a threshold, then flips high through its positive feedback loops and the cell enters mitosis; the negative loop through the anaphase-promoting complex destroys cyclin and resets it. Raise and lower cyclin by hand to trace the hysteresis loop, change the cell's growth rate to see the period change, and apply a DNA-damage checkpoint that holds the switch off.
takeaway: A cell divides when a bistable switch flips, not when a timer runs out: positive feedback makes the decision sharp and hard to reverse, and checkpoints work by holding the switch below its threshold.
needs: Tyson 1991 cyclin-Cdc2 model (BioModels BIOMD0000000005, CC0) or the Novak-Tyson 1993 model as curated in BioModels (CC0).
pitfall: The cycle is not a clock that ticks regardless of state; in the model it is a relaxation oscillator built on a bistable switch, and the page must show the switch flipping, not a smooth sine wave.
why: Tyson & Novak, 'Cell Cycle Vignettes: Bistability and Oscillations' (Virginia Tech teaching note): https://www.biol.vt.edu/content/dam/biol_vt_edu/faculty/tyson/Bistability%20and%20Oscillations.pdf
overlapWith: cancer: that page lets cells divide too often by mutation; this one shows the machinery that decides when a single cell divides, which cancer's mutations break.
needsSource: BioModels curated models, CC0.

title: Central pattern generators
interaction: Connect two neuron models with mutual inhibition and give them a steady, unpatterned drive; they fall into alternating bursts, the half-centre oscillator. Change the drive to speed the rhythm, swap the burst-ending mechanism (adaptation versus post-inhibitory rebound), then chain twenty such pairs along a lamprey's spine with asymmetric coupling: a wave of contraction travels down the body and the fish swims; reverse the coupling bias and it swims backward.
takeaway: Rhythmic movement does not need a rhythmic command: two cells that inhibit each other turn a constant signal into alternation, and a chain of them makes a travelling wave.
pitfall: The half-centre model is a model: lamprey experiments show left-right phasing can survive midline lesions, so the page must present it as the classic mechanism, not the settled one.
why: Model repository rather than a syllabus: lamprey swimming CPG reference implementation in the Nengo model zoo, https://zoo.nengo.ai/submissions/lamprey/index.html (no curriculum signal found in this round).
overlapWith: neurons: that page fires one neuron and sums inputs on the next; this one wires neurons into a circuit whose output is a rhythm none of them has alone.
needsSource: none

title: Circadian clocks
interaction: Run a clock gene that represses its own transcription through a delay (a Goodwin-type loop, with the Leloup-Goldbeter model for the real gene names) and watch mRNA and protein chase each other in a cycle close to 24 hours in constant darkness. Add a light input to the degradation term and the clock locks to the day; shift the light schedule by eight hours and count how many days the phase takes to catch up, eastward versus westward; shorten the delay and the rhythm stops.
takeaway: A gene that switches itself off with a delay oscillates on its own, and daylight does not drive that rhythm but nudges it into step, which is why jet lag takes days to resolve.
needs: Leloup & Goldbeter circadian model as curated in BioModels (CC0); the Goodwin oscillator needs no data.
pitfall: The rhythm persists without any external cue: the page must show free-running oscillation in constant darkness, and must not show the clock as a response to sunrise.
why: MPI MiS course on mathematical modelling of circadian rhythms: https://www.mis.mpg.de/events/event/mathematical-modeling-of-circadian-rhythms
overlapWith: oscillations-resonance: that page is a mass on a spring driven by a force; this is a limit-cycle oscillator made of a delayed negative feedback loop, entrained rather than driven.
needsSource: BioModels curated models, CC0.

title: The coalescent
interaction: Sample ten gene copies from a population and step backwards one generation at a time: each copy picks a parent at random, two lineages that pick the same parent merge, and the genealogy grows down to a single ancestor with its branch lengths. Rerun to see how much the tree varies, change the population size and watch the time to the common ancestor scale with it, and sprinkle mutations on the branches to produce the sample's sequence differences. Squeeze the population through a bottleneck and see the genealogy and the diversity collapse.
takeaway: The pattern of differences in a sample of DNA sequences is the shadow of a random genealogy, and reading that genealogy backwards tells you how large the population was and when it shrank.
pitfall: The most recent common ancestor of a sample is not the first human or a single couple; different genes have different ancestors at different times, and the page should show two loci with different trees.
why: coalesceR, a pedagogical R package for teaching the basics of coalescent theory: https://rdrr.io/rforge/coalesceR
overlapWith: population-genetics: that page runs time forward for a whole population; this one runs it backward for a sample, which is how real sequence data are read.
needsSource: none

title: DNA sequencing & genome assembly
interaction: Sequence a real virus: run a Sanger reaction and sort its fluorescent fragments by length into a chromatogram, then switch to shotgun reads of the whole phiX174 genome and assemble them yourself. Choose read length, coverage and k, watch the de Bruijn graph form from k-mers and collapse into contigs, see repeats tangle the graph and sequencing errors sprout dead ends, and compare the assembly with the true genome.
takeaway: A genome is never read in one piece: it is read as many short overlapping fragments and recovered by a graph algorithm whose success depends on coverage, read length and the genome's repeats.
needs: The phiX174 genome (GenBank NC_001422, 5,386 bases; NCBI places no restrictions on reuse of GenBank records).
pitfall: Sequencing does not read a chromosome end to end; the page must show that short reads lose information in repeats longer than a read, which no amount of coverage recovers.
why: NUS CS4330 lecture 'Practical de Bruijn graph assembly' (a standard bioinformatics-course exercise is assembling phiX174): https://www.comp.nus.edu.sg/~wongls/courses/cs4330/2024/12-practical-dbg-assembly.pdf
overlapWith: crispr: that page cuts DNA at a matched site; this one reads DNA, and its algorithmic core (graphs of overlapping k-mers) has no counterpart in the catalogue.
needsSource: GenBank NC_001422, no reuse restrictions (NCBI policy).

title: Epigenetic memory
interaction: Run a row of nucleosomes that carry a silencing or an activating mark; each marked nucleosome recruits enzymes that convert others, including non-neighbours, and every cell division dilutes the marks by half. Set the recruitment strength and feedback range and watch the row lock into all-silent or all-active and hold that state through dozens of divisions; weaken the cooperativity and the memory decays; force the region silent with a transient pulse and see the state persist after the pulse is gone.
takeaway: A cell can remember a decision without changing its DNA: marks on chromatin that recruit their own copiers form a bistable system that survives being halved at each division.
pitfall: Most chromatin marks are reset between generations; the page must not slide from cellular memory into inheritance of acquired characteristics across organisms.
why: Lecture video rather than a syllabus: math-institute lecture on the Dodd-Sneppen nucleosome-modification model of epigenetic memory, https://mathinstitutes.org/videos/4418 (no curriculum signal found in this round).
overlapWith: dna-to-protein: that page reads a gene; this one decides whether the gene stays readable at all, through marks on the packaging rather than the sequence (model of Dodd et al. 2007).
needsSource: none

title: Evolutionary game theory
interaction: Set the payoffs of a hawk-dove contest and release a population of players; replicator dynamics pulls the share of hawks to the mixed equilibrium that neither strategy can invade, drawn as a flow on a line. Switch to the prisoner's dilemma and watch cooperators die out, then place the players on a grid where they meet neighbours and see clusters of cooperators survive; add relatedness between players and find the cost-to-benefit ratio at which helping kin pays, Hamilton's rule.
takeaway: When fitness depends on what others do, the winning strategy is the one that cannot be invaded rather than the one that scores most, and cooperation survives only when cooperators meet each other more often than chance.
pitfall: Evolutionary stability does not mean the population is at its best: hawks persist even though a population of doves would score higher, and the page must show that the equilibrium is not the optimum.
why: ELTE course on evolutionary game theory (hawk-dove, replicator dynamics, ESS, altruism): https://neptun.elte.hu/MobilityCourses/Course/evojatsb22em
overlapWith: evolution: that page's fitness is fixed by the environment; here fitness depends on what the rest of the population does, which produces equilibria that selection on a fixed landscape never does. It also covers the biological half of the Reserve item 'Game theory' (replicator dynamics, ESS), leaving classical game theory to a math lens.
needsSource: none

title: Noise in gene expression
interaction: Run a single gene with the Gillespie algorithm: the promoter flicks on and off, each on-period fires a burst of mRNAs, each mRNA a burst of proteins. Set the switching, transcription, translation and decay rates and watch the protein count jitter in one cell while a histogram across a thousand cells widens or narrows. Add a second identical reporter to the same cell and plot one against the other: scatter along the diagonal is shared, extrinsic noise; scatter across it is the gene's own, intrinsic noise.
takeaway: Genetically identical cells in the same environment differ because their molecules are counted in tens and made in bursts, and a two-reporter scatter plot separates the randomness of the gene itself from the randomness of the cell around it.
pitfall: Noise does not simply average out at higher expression: bursty expression keeps the Fano factor above one, so the model must produce bursts, not a Poisson stream of single proteins.
why: LMU Munich 'Biophysics of Systems' lecture on stochastic gene expression (Elowitz 2002 two-reporter experiment): https://www2.physik.uni-muenchen.de/lehre/vorlesungen/wise_20_21/Biophysics_of_Systems/04b_StochasticGenes_2E.pdf
overlapWith: central-limit-theorem: that page shows averages converging; here the counts are so small that the fluctuations are the biology, and bursts keep them from averaging out.
needsSource: none

title: Synthetic gene circuits: toggle switch & repressilator
interaction: Wire promoters, repressors and a fluorescent reporter into a circuit on a plasmid, set repression strength, cooperativity and degradation rates, and run it. Two genes that repress each other make a switch that a pulse of inducer flips and that stays flipped; three in a ring make an oscillator whose fluorescence blinks, and the reader finds the parameter region where the blinking dies. A stochastic solver shows the same circuit jitter in a single cell.
takeaway: Two genes that repress each other remember a state and three in a ring keep time, so the logic of a cell's control can be built from a handful of parts, and whether a circuit works depends on the numbers, not just the wiring.
needs: Repressilator model of Elowitz & Leibler 2000 as curated in BioModels (BIOMD0000000012, CC0); toggle-switch equations and parameters from Gardner, Cantor & Collins 2000 (published values, no dataset).
pitfall: Oscillation is not guaranteed by the ring: with weak repression or low cooperativity the repressilator settles to a steady state, so the page must show the dead region rather than a circuit that always blinks.
why: Yale 'Biologic' module teaching the toggle switch and repressilator to biology and premedical students: https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.3126
overlapWith: logic-gates: that page composes ideal digital gates; here each gate is a leaky, continuous repressor with a time constant, and the question is which wirings still switch or oscillate.
needsSource: BioModels curated repressilator (CC0); toggle-switch parameters from the paper, no dataset needed.

title: The genetic code's error tolerance
interaction: Hover any codon in the genetic-code table to see which amino acids one base change can reach, coloured by how different their chemistry is, and total a cost for the whole code. Then press shuffle: the page draws thousands of random codes that keep the same block structure, scores each one, and builds a histogram with the standard code marked; change the cost measure (polarity, volume, charge) or the mutation bias and watch where the standard code lands.
takeaway: Most single-base errors in the real code swap an amino acid for a chemically similar one, and among random codes with the same structure only a tiny fraction do better, though how tiny depends on what you measure.
needs: Amino-acid polar requirement (Woese 1966) and other physico-chemical scales from the published literature; the standard code table (public domain).
pitfall: The 'one in a million' figure holds only for polar requirement with a transition/transversion bias; with volume or charge the standard code is far less special, and the page must not present the code as uniquely optimal.
why: Freeland & Hurst 1998 as a course reading in Swarthmore Phys 120: https://www.sccs.swarthmore.edu/users/08/bblonder/phys120/docs/freeland.pdf
overlapWith: dna-to-protein: that page shows what one mutation does to one protein; this one scores the whole table against every alternative code.
needsSource: Published amino-acid property scales (literature values); code table public domain.

title: Gene regulation & the lac operon
interaction: Set the lactose and glucose in a bacterium's medium and watch an ODE model of the lac operon respond: the repressor leaves the operator when an inducer is present, CAP recruits the polymerase only when glucose is low, and the permease the operon makes imports more inducer. Sweep the inducer up and then down to trace the hysteresis loop, and grow a culture on both sugars to see the diauxic pause when the glucose runs out.
takeaway: A bacterium switches a set of genes on only when their product is useful and nothing better is around, and positive feedback through its own transporter turns that switch into a memory: the same inducer level can leave the operon on or off depending on where it came from.
pitfall: Bistability and hysteresis were measured with the gratuitous inducer TMG; with plain lactose the loop is weak or absent because lactose is also consumed, so the page must not present lactose itself as a memory switch.
why: MIT OCW 7.01SC Fundamentals of Biology, module 'Gene Regulation and the Lac Operon': https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/7-01sc-fundamentals-of-biology-fall-2011/resources/molecbio_sess5
overlapWith: dna-to-protein: that page reads one gene into a protein; this one is about when the gene is read at all, as a dynamical switch with feedback (model of Ozbudak et al. 2004).
needsSource: none

title: Luria-Delbruck: mutations before selection
interaction: Step through the 1943 experiment: grow twenty cultures from single cells for a chosen number of generations at a chosen mutation rate, plate them all on a phage lawn, and count the survivors. If mutations arose only on contact with the phage the counts would be Poisson and nearly equal; instead a few plates hold hundreds of mutants, the jackpots, because a mutation that happened early was inherited by a whole clone. Replay with mutations induced at plating to see the Poisson alternative, and estimate the mutation rate from the fraction of empty plates.
takeaway: Mutations happen before and regardless of the challenge they will later face, and the wild spread between replicate cultures is the signature of that.
pitfall: The jackpot distribution does not show that the environment induces mutations; it shows the opposite, and the page must make the Poisson alternative explicit so the reader sees it fail.
why: 'Fascination with Fluctuation: Luria and Delbruck's Legacy', on the experiment in undergraduate mathematics education (University of Delaware): https://udspace.udel.edu/items/2837763f-b87a-465a-9701-2b96405d98f5/full
overlapWith: evolution: that page's pitfall says mutations do not arise because they are needed; this one is the experiment that proved it, run as a statistics-of-clones simulation.
needsSource: none

title: Membrane transport & the resting potential
interaction: Drag the ion concentrations on each side of a membrane and the permeability of each channel type, and watch ions cross while the voltage settles: with only potassium channels open it sits at the Nernst potential, and as sodium leaks in it drifts toward the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz value shown live. Switch the sodium-potassium pump off and watch the gradients, the voltage and the cell's volume decay over simulated hours; then dilute the outside solution and see water follow the ions.
takeaway: A cell's voltage is a weighted average of each ion's equilibrium potential, weighted by how permeable the membrane is to it, and holding that voltage and the cell's volume costs a steady stream of ATP through the pump.
pitfall: The pump's direct electrical contribution to the resting potential is a few millivolts; the voltage comes mostly from the potassium gradient the pump maintains, and the page must not show the pump charging the membrane like a battery.
why: University of Kent LearnSci module on membrane potential, with Nernst and GHK calculation as learning outcomes: https://www.learnsci.com/resources/membrane-potential
overlapWith: neurons: that page fires an action potential on top of a resting voltage it takes for granted; this one builds that resting voltage from gradients, permeabilities and the pump.
needsSource: none

title: Metabolic networks & flux balance
interaction: Open a map of central carbon metabolism (glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway, the TCA cycle, fermentation, respiration) with every reaction's stoichiometry, and choose what the cell maximises and what it may take up. A linear-programme solver in the browser finds the flux through every reaction, drawn as arrow widths; cut the oxygen supply and watch flux reroute to fermentation, knock out a gene and see whether growth survives by a detour, and sweep the glucose uptake to trace growth rate against it.
takeaway: Knowing only which reactions exist and that nothing accumulates, a cell's best possible division of flux can be computed, and the network's detours are what make most single knockouts survivable.
needs: A documented core E. coli network. The BiGG e_coli_core model is free for educational and non-profit use but not openly licensed (UC Regents terms), so build the network from textbook stoichiometry with references, or from a CC0 BioModels-curated central-metabolism model.
pitfall: FBA predicts a bound, not a measurement: it has no kinetics and no regulation, so the page must say that the optimum is a hypothesis about what the cell maximises and that real fluxes can differ.
why: UCSD Systems Biology Research Group FBA tutorial with the core E. coli model: https://sbrg.ucsd.edu/node/61
overlapWith: respiration-atp: that page follows one glucose through the pathways; this one treats the whole network at once and asks how flux divides among all routes.
needsSource: BiGG e_coli_core is non-commercial only (weak); textbook stoichiometry needs no licence; BioModels is CC0.

title: The microbiome as an ecosystem
interaction: Run a gut community of ten bacterial groups with the interaction matrix Stein et al. inferred from mouse data; it settles to a stable mix. Dose it with an antibiotic for a chosen number of days and watch some groups crash and others bloom; introduce C. difficile before, during and after the course and see it fail, invade, or take hold; stop the antibiotic and find that the community does not always return, then transplant a healthy community to push it back.
takeaway: A gut community is a web of competition and support with more than one stable state, so a disturbance can tip it into a new one that persists after the disturbance is gone.
needs: Generalized Lotka-Volterra interaction matrix and antibiotic susceptibilities from Stein et al. 2013, PLOS Computational Biology (CC BY).
pitfall: The parameters come from mice and one antibiotic, and gLV fits are uncertain; the page must say the model illustrates the dynamics and is not a prediction for a human gut.
why: Demand: public coverage of ecological modelling of the gut microbiota (Gut Microbiota for Health): https://www.gutmicrobiotaforhealth.com/ecological-modeling-of-intestinal-microbiota/ ; model source is Stein et al. 2013, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003388 (no curriculum signal found in this round).
overlapWith: ecosystems: that page has one predator, one prey and a small food web; here a ten-group community with alternative stable states, driven by real inferred interactions and perturbed by an antibiotic.
needsSource: PLOS Computational Biology article and supplementary parameters, CC BY.

title: Molecular motors: how kinesin walks
interaction: Watch a kinesin dimer take 8 nm steps along a microtubule while a cargo bead trails it in a simulated optical trap; each step waits a random time set by ATP binding and hydrolysis, so the trace is a staircase with jittery dwells. Lower the ATP concentration and the dwells lengthen; raise the backward load and the motor slows, stalls near 7 pN and starts stepping backward; plot velocity against force and against ATP and compare the shapes with published single-molecule curves.
takeaway: A molecular motor is not a tiny engine with a steady push: it takes random, thermally driven steps that ATP hydrolysis biases forward, and a load of a few piconewtons is enough to stop it.
needs: Discrete-state mechanochemical model and parameters from Fisher & Kolomeisky 2001 (PNAS, published values); a kinesin structure from the Protein Data Bank (CC0) for the illustration.
pitfall: Do not draw the motor as pulled by a constant force or sliding smoothly; at this scale thermal motion dominates, and the forward bias comes from rectifying it with chemical energy.
why: Workshop lecture notes rather than a syllabus: BIRS lecture on molecular-motor stepping citing Kolomeisky & Fisher as the standard model, https://stats.birs.ca/workshops/2018/18w5144/files/fricks.pdf (no curriculum signal found in this round).
overlapWith: respiration-atp: that page makes ATP with a rotary motor; this one spends ATP to move along a track, with the stochastic stepping shown rather than a turning rotor.
needsSource: Model parameters from the published paper; PDB structures are CC0.

title: Morphogen gradients & positional information
interaction: Drag the production rate, diffusion constant and lifetime of a morphogen made at one end of an embryo and watch its concentration profile settle into an exponential whose length scale the page reports. Set two or three thresholds and the cells paint themselves in bands, Wolpert's French flag; double the embryo's length to see the bands fail to scale, then switch on a scaling mechanism and compare; add noise to see which boundaries are robust.
takeaway: A cell can learn where it is from how much of one substance reaches it, and the shape of that gradient, set by diffusion and decay, decides where the boundaries fall.
pitfall: The synthesis-diffusion-degradation model is a working hypothesis and the Bicoid gradient's formation is still debated; the page must present the exponential as what the model predicts and say where it is tested.
why: Stanford course on morphogenesis listing morphogen gradients and Turing patterns: https://bulletin.stanford.edu/courses/2126934
overlapWith: the-cell: that page zooms into one cell; this one shows how thousands of cells in a row find out which part of the body they are making.
needsSource: none

title: Phylogenetics: building the tree of life
interaction: Pick a handful of species, align their cytochrome b sequences and watch the page count differences into a distance matrix. Build the tree by UPGMA, merging the closest pair step by step, then rebuild it by neighbour joining and see where the two disagree; speed up one lineage's clock and watch UPGMA put it in the wrong place; switch to a parsimony score and drag branches to try to beat the algorithm.
takeaway: A tree of life is not observed but computed from the differences between sequences, and a method's assumptions, such as a constant rate of change, decide which tree it finds.
needs: Mitochondrial cytochrome b (or 16S rRNA) sequences for a dozen species from GenBank (NCBI places no restrictions on reuse); the species' accepted relationships from the Open Tree of Life synthetic tree for comparison (reported CC0, to confirm on the project site).
pitfall: Humans are not at the 'top' of the tree and no living species is the ancestor of another: the page must let the reader rotate nodes to show that only the branching order carries information.
why: CUHK BMEG3102 Bioinformatics tutorial on molecular phylogenetics (UPGMA, NJ, parsimony, likelihood): https://webarchive.lib.cuhk.edu.hk/20210407143348mp_/http:/www.cse.cuhk.edu.hk/~qdou/bmeg3102/tutorials/BMEG3102_2021Spring_Tutorial06_MolecularPhylogenetics_CUHK.pdf
overlapWith: deep-time: that page scrubs a dated timeline of life; this one computes the branching order from today's sequences and has no dates until a clock is assumed.
needsSource: GenBank sequences, no reuse restrictions (load-bearing); Open Tree of Life reported CC0, to confirm.

title: Population genetics: drift & selection
interaction: Run a hundred Wright-Fisher populations at once as allele-frequency traces: with no selection they wander and fix at random, faster in small populations; with a selection coefficient s they bend toward fixation, and a counter shows how often a new beneficial mutation is lost anyway, approaching Kimura's 2s. Set dominance to see recessive alleles hide from selection, and compare the Hardy-Weinberg genotype frequencies with the simulated ones each generation.
takeaway: Allele frequencies change by chance as well as by selection, and in a small population chance wins: most beneficial mutations are lost before selection can act on them.
pitfall: Hardy-Weinberg is not 'evolution stops': it is the one-generation baseline that shows which forces are absent, and drift is not selection by another name; the page must keep them separate.
why: Cal State LA BIOL 415 Population Genetics syllabus (Hardy-Weinberg, drift, effective size, selection, coalescent): https://www.calstatela.edu/sites/default/files/syllabibiol415.pdf
overlapWith: evolution: that page shifts a trait distribution with predators and food; this one tracks a single allele's frequency and separates chance from selection with explicit N and s.
needsSource: none

title: Origin of life & the error threshold
interaction: Run a pool of self-copying RNA strings on a fitness peak with a chosen copying error rate per base and a chosen length: below a threshold the population clusters around the best sequence as a cloud of mutants, above it the information melts into random sequences. Lengthen the genome and watch the threshold fall, then let the strings evolve a copying enzyme with better fidelity and see the longest sustainable genome grow; close with parasites exploiting a shared replicase and compartments containing them.
takeaway: A replicator can carry only as much information as its copying accuracy allows, so the first genomes had to be short, and getting longer required evolving better copiers first.
pitfall: The error threshold has no single agreed definition and the RNA world is a hypothesis; the page must not present the simulation as a reconstruction of how life began.
why: Wikipedia, 'Error threshold (evolution)' (Eigen's paradox and the RNA world): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Error_threshold_(evolution)
overlapWith: error-correction: that page adds redundancy to a message to survive noise; here the message is a genome that must copy itself through noise, and the question is how long it can be.
needsSource: none

title: Quorum sensing
interaction: Grow a colony of bacteria on a grid; each cell secretes an autoinducer that diffuses and decays, and once its receptor sees enough of it the LuxI/LuxR positive feedback switches the cell's light genes on. Watch the colony stay dark until a sharp density is reached and then light up together; shrink the chamber, slow the diffusion, or add an enzyme that destroys the signal, and find the population at which the switch flips.
takeaway: Bacteria count themselves by releasing a molecule and listening for it, and positive feedback turns a gradual rise in signal into a collective, all-or-none switch at a threshold density.
pitfall: The signal measures confinement and diffusion as much as cell number: a single cell in a tiny sealed space can trigger its own switch, and the page must show that.
why: iGEM Wageningen UR 2017 quorum-sensing model (LuxI/LuxR ODEs with positive feedback): https://2017.igem.org/Team:Wageningen_UR/Model/QS
overlapWith: crispr: both are bacterial systems, but this page is about cells coordinating by diffusion and feedback rather than remembering viruses.
needsSource: none

title: Rubisco, photorespiration & C4 plants
interaction: Run the Farquhar-von Caemmerer-Berry model of a leaf: set CO2, oxygen, light and temperature and watch Rubisco split its time between fixing CO2 and wastefully grabbing O2, with the assimilation curve against CO2 drawn live and the limiting step marked. Raise the temperature and watch photorespiration eat the gain; then switch the leaf to a C4 anatomy that pumps CO2 into the bundle sheath, or to CAM that opens its stomata at night, and compare carbon gain and water loss across a hot day.
takeaway: The enzyme at the base of nearly all food confuses oxygen with CO2, and C4 and CAM plants are two engineering fixes that concentrate CO2 around it or move its work to the night.
needs: Rubisco kinetic constants and their temperature dependence (von Caemmerer 2000; Bernacchi et al. 2001; published values).
pitfall: C4 is not 'better' photosynthesis: at cool temperatures and low light its extra ATP cost makes it lose to C3, and the page must show the crossover.
why: POGIL classroom activity 'C4 and CAM Photosynthesis' for upper-level plant physiology: https://pac.pogil.org/index.php/pac/article/view/557
overlapWith: photosynthesis: that page follows photons to sugar in one chloroplast; this one is the enzyme kinetics of the carbon-fixing step and the leaf-level consequences of its oxygen mistake.
needsSource: Published kinetic parameters only.

title: The segmentation clock
interaction: Run a strip of cells along a growing embryo axis, each with a delayed negative-feedback oscillator (the her1/her7 model) and a wavefront that sweeps back as the tail grows and freezes each cell's phase when it passes. Watch waves of expression sweep forward and somites pinch off one per cycle; speed the clock or the wavefront and measure how somite size changes, then couple neighbouring oscillators through Notch and remove the coupling to see the stripes blur.
takeaway: A body's segments are counted out by a clock: every cycle of an oscillator, a moving front freezes one more block of cells, so segment size equals clock period times front speed.
pitfall: Somite size is not set by a prepattern of fixed stripes; the page must show that changing the clock period changes the size, which a prepattern could not.
why: Teaching material rather than a syllabus: tutorial review 'Waves, patterns and bifurcations' on the vertebrate segmentation clock, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.00457 (no curriculum signal found in this round).
overlapWith: turing-patterns: both make periodic stripes, but here the period is in time and is converted into space by a moving front, with a different model (Lewis 2003 delay oscillator) and a different control.
needsSource: none

title: Cell signalling: cascades & ultrasensitivity
interaction: Apply a graded dose of signal to the top of a three-tier kinase cascade (the Huang-Ferrell MAPK model) and plot each tier's active fraction against dose: the first tier responds gently, the last switches almost all-or-none. Change the phosphatase levels, remove the second phosphorylation site, or close a feedback loop and watch the response steepen, flatten or become bistable; a sketch places the cascade between a receptor and the nucleus.
takeaway: Stacking enzyme steps with double phosphorylation turns a gentle input into a sharp threshold, so a cell can make a decision from a graded signal without any single cooperative molecule.
needs: Huang & Ferrell 1996 MAPK cascade model as curated in BioModels (BIOMD0000000009, CC0).
pitfall: The steep response is not cooperativity in hemoglobin's sense: no enzyme in the model is allosteric, and the page must attribute the Hill coefficient of four to five to the cascade's structure.
why: BioModels/COPASI course tutorial built on the Huang-Ferrell model: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/biomodels/courses/20160706/tutorial_handout.pdf
overlapWith: homeostasis: that page is whole-body hormone feedback; this one is the enzyme-level machinery inside one cell that turns a signal into a decision.
needsSource: BioModels curated model, CC0.

title: Speciation
interaction: Split a population in two with a barrier and let each half accumulate its own mutations in a set of interacting genes, each change neutral or useful at home. Lift the barrier after a chosen time and cross the two: hybrid fitness falls as pairs of alleles that never met prove incompatible (Dobzhansky-Muller), and a counter shows incompatibilities growing faster than linearly with time. Let gene flow leak through the barrier to see divergence stall, and add selection against hybrids to watch reinforcement finish the job.
takeaway: Two populations become species not by one changing into something new but by each drifting along its own path until their genes no longer work together, and the barrier between them grows faster the longer they are apart.
pitfall: No single mutation makes a new species and no individual is 'the first' of one; incompatibilities arise between alleles that were each harmless where they evolved.
why: MERLOT peer-reviewed classroom activity modelling the Dobzhansky-Muller process: https://awscbdev.merlot.org/merlot/viewMaterial.htm?id=851638
overlapWith: evolution: that page adapts one population to its environment; this one follows two separated populations and measures the barrier that grows between them.
needsSource: none

title: Synaptic plasticity: Hebbian learning & STDP
interaction: Pair a presynaptic and a postsynaptic spike at a chosen interval and watch the synapse's weight grow when the input leads by a few milliseconds and shrink when it lags, tracing the STDP window over sixty pairings. Then feed a neuron twenty inputs with different timings and let STDP run: the earliest reliable inputs win, the rest fade, and a pattern hidden in noise is picked out. Switch to a plain Hebbian rule without timing and watch the weights run away until a normalisation is added.
takeaway: Synapses strengthen when the input helps cause the output and weaken when it arrives too late, so a neuron learns to respond to the earliest predictors of its own firing, with no teacher.
needs: STDP window shape and time constants from Bi & Poo 1998 (published values; the page uses the standard exponential rule, no dataset shipped).
pitfall: 'Cells that fire together wire together' is incomplete: order matters, and a rule with no depression or no bound makes every weight grow without limit; the page must show the depression side and the need for normalisation.
why: HSE course 'Mathematical Models of Brain Neural Networks' listing Hodgkin-Huxley, synaptic plasticity and STDP: https://www.hse.ru/edu/courses/835249132
overlapWith: neural-networks: that page adjusts weights by gradient descent against a target; here the weights change by a local rule from spike timing alone, with no error signal.
needsSource: Published parameter values only.

title: Turing patterns
interaction: Run an activator-inhibitor reaction-diffusion system on a grid from near-uniform noise and watch spots or stripes crystallise. Change the ratio of the two diffusion rates and the pattern appears only once the inhibitor spreads much faster than the activator; change the reaction rates to move from spots to stripes to labyrinths; grow the domain and extra stripes insert themselves, and taper the grid into a tail to see spots become bands as it narrows.
takeaway: Two chemicals, one that makes more of itself and a faster-spreading one that suppresses it, can turn a uniform field into regular spots or stripes with no blueprint, at a wavelength set by rates alone.
pitfall: Not every stripe in nature is a Turing pattern; the page should name where the mechanism is supported (digits, hair follicles, fish skin) and must not claim it for zebra stripes or fingerprints without saying that is contested.
why: University of Manchester undergraduate brochure feature on the Turing pattern: https://www.scieng.manchester.ac.uk/undergraduate-brochures/2024/the-turing-pattern/
overlapWith: chaos-fractals: that page grows patterns by iterating a map; here they grow from a PDE with a definite wavelength, and the control is the diffusion ratio.
needsSource: none

title: Viral replication inside a host
interaction: Infect a host in the Perelson model: virus enters target cells, infected cells bud new virions and die, and viral load climbs to a plateau where production and clearance balance. Start a drug that blocks new infections and watch the load fall in two phases whose slopes give the half-lives of free virus (hours) and of infected cells (about a day); stop the drug early and it rebounds; let the virus mutate at a chosen rate and see a resistant strain take over under one drug but not under three.
takeaway: A steady viral load is not a quiet infection but a furious balance of billions of virions made and cleared every day, which is why resistance evolves so fast and why combination therapy works.
pitfall: The two-phase decay and its half-lives are estimates fitted to patients by Perelson et al.; the page must present them as fitted values, not as constants of the virus.
why: q-bio Summer School 'Viral Dynamics' (Perelson's lecture 'How to model a viral infection within the host'): https://q-bio.org/wiki/The_Seventh_q-bio_Summer_School:_Viral_Dynamics
overlapWith: epidemics: that page counts infected people; this one counts infected cells inside one person, where the same kind of equations give half-lives rather than reproduction numbers.
needsSource: none
